REFUTED on the speaker, not on the words. The wording is Jowett's and I confirmed it myself rather than trusting the verifier: I downloaded Project Gutenberg 1572 (Title: Timaeus, Author: Plato, Translator: Benjamin Jowett) and found the sentence at one place only in the dialogue proper, running 'Wherefore he resolved to have a moving image of eternity, and when he set in order the heaven, he made this image eternal but moving according to number, while eternity itself rests in unity; and this image we call time.' Character for character, stop for stop, semicolon and all. The verifier's other claim also holds: the only other occurrence of the phrase in the file is in Jowett's own analysis near the front ('also created time, the moving image of eternity, and space'), and the proposal has taken the dialogue, not the introduction. The Stephanus locator is right: the sentence sits between 'Now the nature of the ideal being was everlasting' and 'For there were no days and nights and months and years before the heaven was created', which is 37d.

WHAT BREAKS IT. Rule 5 says a character's line names the speaker in parentheses after the locator, and the brief repeats it as one of the two speaker traps to carry generally: a line spoken by a character is the character's. This is a character's line. I traced the speech tags in the Gutenberg text: the last speaker before the passage is at 'TIMAEUS: Let me tell you then why the creator made this world of generation', and no tag intervenes between that and the sentence, so the whole cosmology, 37d included, is spoken by Timaeus of Locri. Plato is nowhere in his own voice in this dialogue. The card prints the byline from the source line and has no author field, so as proposed it would print 'Plato' over words the dialogue gives to another man, which is the same shape of error the misattribution list rules on for the Aeneid: real, but it is Turnus speaking, so name the speaker or leave it.

THE HOUSE HAS ALREADY DECIDED THIS TWICE. Both shipped Plato lines name the speaker in exactly the place rule 5 asks for: month 05 carries 'Plato, Apology, 38a (Socrates) (trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1892)' and month 07 carries 'Plato, Laches, 192b to c (Laches) (trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1892)'. Month 07 does the same for a personified speaker, 'Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, Prose IV (Philosophy) (trans. H. R. James, 1897)'. A third Plato of the year that silently drops the convention the first two observed is an inconsistency a reader of the year would see, and it is the year's third Plato: shipped.js returns plato at 2 of 3, months 5 and 7, so this line spends the cap.

THE FIX, AND EVERYTHING THAT SURVIVES. betterCitation inserts '(Timaeus)' after the locator and before the translation parenthesis, following the month 05 and month 07 pattern exactly. It is 60 characters, leads with the author's name, carries no dash of any kind and no straight quote. Nothing else about the line needs touching. shipped.js on the exact wording: shipped [], near [], Plato not banned, not at cap. The work is fourth century BC and the translation 1892, so scope is clear: not scripture, not film, not lyric, not proverb, not business, not oratory, nothing after 1999. Nothing here needs a content warning. Tag Philosophy is the form of the work. The quotation ends in a full stop, is prose and is kept as prose. And the line is the best fit for the month I was shown: a moving image of eternity is impermanence given a reason to exist rather than mourned, which is the second half of the August blurb and works at six in the morning. Ship it with the speaker named.
